---
title: "Small Binomial"
description: "Zero concentration, skewness, and a persistent lattice"
---

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
source("../R/populations.R")
source("../R/diagnostics.R")
source("../R/simulation.R")
source("../R/plots.R")
library(ggplot2)
population <- get_population("binomial")
diagnostics <- read.csv("../results/diagnostics.csv")
page_results <- diagnostics[diagnostics$population == "binomial", ]
bands <- read.csv("../results/calibration_bands.csv")
selected_n <- c(1, 30, 200)
simulation <- simulate_population(population, selected_n, B = 10000L, seed = 631L, keep_means = TRUE)
```

## 1. Question and prediction

For $X \sim Binomial(5,0.10)$, most individual values are zero and the remaining mass stretches right. I expected both skewness and lattice spacing to delay a useful Normal approximation.

## 2. Parent population

```{r}
#| label: fig-binomial-parent
#| fig-cap: "The Binomial(5, 0.10) parent places most probability at zero and rapidly less at larger counts. Both zero concentration and right skew challenge the approximation."
#| fig-alt: "A bar chart dominated by outcome zero, with rapidly decreasing bars through five."
plot_parent_population(population)
```

## 3. Theory before simulation

The parent mean is $5(0.10)=0.5$ and variance is $5(0.10)(0.90)=0.45$. Independent identical observations are bounded, so the ordinary CLT applies and

$$
SE(\bar X_n)=\sqrt{\frac{0.45}{n}}.
$$

Discreteness does not violate the theorem, but it can remain visible in finite samples.

## 4. Simulation design

The grid is dense from $n=1$ to 200, then checks 300 and 500 for stability. Every grid point uses 10,000 means and seed 631. The independent second-seed check is reserved for Exponential, the genuinely most borderline finite-variance case.

## 5. Numerical evidence

```{r}
#| label: tbl-binomial-diagnostics
#| tbl-cap: "Small-Binomial diagnostics around n = 200. Skewness reaches the practical band while Q-Q RMSE remains elevated by the lattice."
shown <- page_results[page_results$n %in% c(75, 100, 125, 150, 200, 300, 500), c("n", "mean_error", "relative_se_error", "skewness", "excess_kurtosis", "qq_rmse")]
names(shown) <- c("n", "Center error", "Relative SE error", "Skewness", "Excess kurtosis", "Q-Q RMSE")
knitr::kable(shown, digits = 4, row.names = FALSE)
```

At $n=200$, skewness is `r sprintf("%.3f", page_results$skewness[page_results$n == 200])`, below the 0.10 guidance, and the empirical SE is within `r sprintf("%.2f%%", 100 * page_results$relative_se_error[page_results$n == 200])` of theory.

## 6. Shape across sample sizes

```{r}
#| label: fig-binomial-sampling
#| fig-cap: "The parent-like sampling distribution at n = 1 gives way to a skewed lattice at n = 30 and a nearly symmetric, fine-grained bell at n = 200. Dark curves are theoretical Normal references."
#| fig-alt: "Three histograms showing a zero-heavy discrete shape becoming a narrow, nearly symmetric bell."
plot_sampling_distributions(simulation$means, population, selected_n)
```

## 7. Q-Q evidence

```{r}
#| label: fig-binomial-qq
#| fig-cap: "Q-Q curvature and steps both shrink with n. At n = 200, small steps remain even though the overall line is straight enough for a practical approximation."
#| fig-alt: "Three Q-Q panels becoming straighter and more finely stepped with larger sample size."
plot_qq_comparison(simulation$means, population, selected_n)
```

## 8. Diagnostic trajectory and standard error

```{r}
#| label: fig-binomial-trajectory
#| fig-cap: "Skewness and excess kurtosis settle faster than Q-Q RMSE. The gap records a fine lattice that remains measurable after the global shape becomes useful."
#| fig-alt: "Three diagnostic trajectories declining at different rates across Binomial sample sizes."
plot_diagnostic_trajectory(page_results, population, bands)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-binomial-se
#| fig-cap: "Empirical and theoretical standard errors nearly overlap across the grid. As in the other skewed case, precision stabilizes before shape."
#| fig-alt: "Two nearly overlapping standard-error curves declining with Binomial sample size."
plot_se_comparison(page_results, population)
```

## 9. Decision and disagreement

**Decision: $n=200$.** The center, SE, global histogram, and skewness support a practical Normal approximation, and the judgment persists at $n=300$ and $n=500$. Q-Q RMSE remains above the Normal calibration because standardized sample means still occupy a lattice. That disagreement is real and matters most for fine tail or continuity-sensitive calculations.

## 10. Limitation and surprise

The threshold is specific to size 5 and probability 0.10. A rarer-success Binomial would converge more slowly. The surprise is that the discrete grid remains measurable after the histogram already looks convincingly bell-shaped.
